name: GoMotion AI
tagline: AI tool that turns video or prompts into animated motion, aimed at creators who do not want to keyframe by hand.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The interface here is a thin wrapper around the part you cannot one-shot: trained motion models and the GPUs that run them. An agent can absolutely build you an upload form, a job queue, and a results gallery in an afternoon, and that gets you a very nice empty box. The actual output quality comes from model weights plus a lot of unglamorous cleanup heuristics, and the open alternatives you can self-host are noticeably rougher than a polished commercial pipeline. If your use case is simple body motion capture from a single video, a local pose-estimation pipeline gets you surprisingly far for free. If you want clean, retargetable, production-usable motion from arbitrary input, you are paying for the models and the render farm, not the UI.
coreLoopDIY: A local Python pipeline that takes an MP4, runs open-source pose estimation on it, and exports a rough skeletal animation you can import into Blender and clean up yourself.
requirements: A machine with a GPU if you want this to finish before you lose interest
Blender installed for import, retargeting, and cleanup
Tolerance for jittery output and manual smoothing
whatYouLose: Model quality: commercial motion models are trained on licensed capture data you do not have
Text-to-motion entirely, open pose estimation only reads existing video
Clean rigs and retargeting that just work on your character instead of a day of bone mapping
Hands, fingers, and facial motion, which is where open pipelines fall apart first
Any kind of speed, local inference on long clips is a coffee-and-then-lunch affair
moatNotes: Motion data is expensive to capture and licensed carefully, which is why the good models are not sitting on a weights hub waiting for you.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the deliverable is believable motion, and believable motion is a model problem, not a software problem. You can replicate every button, the upload, the queue, the preview player, the download, and still ship output that looks like a drunk marionette. The commercial version is paying for licensed capture corpora, retargeting logic refined against thousands of real rigs, and inference hardware that returns a result in a minute instead of forty. For a hobby project the free pipeline is fine. For anything a client sees, the per-render fee is cheaper than your cleanup time.
notes: You can clone the product in a day and the output in approximately never. The moat is licensed motion capture data plus the retargeting cleanup nobody blogs about.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user video-to-animation pipeline. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Python 3.11, uv for dependency management
- MediaPipe Pose (or an equivalent open pose estimator) for 3D landmark extraction
- ffmpeg via subprocess for frame extraction and clip trimming
- Typer for the CLI
- A single-file FastAPI + HTMX local UI on port 8000 for drag-and-drop jobs
- SQLite for job records, stored in ./data/jobs.db

In scope:
- CLI command: motion extract INPUT.mp4 --fps 30 --out out/clip.bvh
- Extract per-frame 3D pose landmarks, map them to a fixed humanoid skeleton, write a valid BVH file
- A temporal smoothing pass: one-euro filter or Savitzky-Golay over joint rotations, with --smooth 0..1
- Foot contact detection and a crude foot-lock pass so the character does not skate
- Render a side-by-side MP4 preview: original video next to a stick-figure playback of the BVH
- Local web UI: drop a video, pick fps and smoothing, watch job status, download BVH and preview
- A Blender import script in scripts/import_bvh.py that loads the BVH and retargets it onto the Rigify sample armature

Out of scope, do not attempt:
- Text-to-motion, hand and finger tracking, facial capture, multi-person tracking
- Any hosted inference, API keys, or paid services
- User auth, sharing, billing

Requirements:
- Everything runs offline after first model download
- Any config lives in .env with a committed .env.example, no hardcoded paths
- README with install steps, one worked example, and an honest Limitations section listing jitter, drift, and missing extremities
- Write out/report.json per job with frame count, dropped-frame count, and mean landmark confidence so the user can tell when the capture is garbage
